A1.justification: Both PDFs describe VideoChat-Flash, with matching HiCo, LongVid, training stages, and NIAH experiments. All supplied text and visual material supports comparison. v1 ends with references; v3 additionally includes Supplementary Material, Sections 6–9.

before.justification: v1 reports original video-understanding, temporal-grounding, NIAH, efficiency, and ablation results in Tables 1–8 and Figures 6–7.

after.justification: v3 retains original empirical results and adds smaller-model evaluations, captioning and image-understanding results, supplementary analyses, and qualitative comparisons.

M1.justification: Section 3.1 explicitly changes timestamp-prompt placement from before the video context in v1 to after it in v3. The core clip compression, token merging, progressive visual dropout, and four training stages remain. Renaming dynamic sampling and specifying its formula do not alone establish another procedural change.

E1.justification: v3 adds video-captioning evaluation labeled AuroraCap in Table 1 and image-understanding evaluation on MMMU and MME in Section 6.3. These extend evaluation beyond v1's video QA, temporal grounding, and NIAH tasks. The existing video benchmarks and LongVid's four source datasets remain.

E2.justification: v3 Table 1 adds VITA1.5, Qwen2.5-VL, and 2B comparators, while removing VideoLLaMA2, IXComposer-2.5, and LongLLaVA from the main benchmark comparison. VideoLLaMA2 reappears in qualitative comparisons. v1 Table 3's specialized grounding comparators, including 2D-TAN, MMN, and UniVTG, are also dropped.

E3.justification: Charades-STA evaluation changes from R@1 at IoU thresholds 0.3/0.5/0.7 to mIoU. v3 adds 2B and InternVideo2-1B configurations and a visual-encoder experiment comparing 2M versus 8M training samples. Its sampling analysis tests upper bounds through 512 frames, whereas v1 Table 4 stops at 128.

E4.justification: Beyond v1's existing ablations, v3 Table 2 examines HiCo, timestamp prompts, and high-resolution post-finetuning within a broader component study. Sampling and encoder analyses are substantially revised. Supplementary Figures 8–9 add layerwise dropout sensitivity and attention diagnostics, and Figures 11–14 add four qualitative comparison cases.

E5.justification: Both versions report point estimates without repeated-run counts, seeds, confidence intervals, error bars, or formal significance tests. The added analyses do not introduce uncertainty reporting.

E6.justification: Corresponding 7B@448 entries are revised: MVBench changes from 73.9 to 74.0, MLVU from 74.5 to 74.7, and VideoMME without subtitles from 64.7 to 65.3. v3 adds 2B, captioning, image, and encoder results and replaces efficiency estimates, without establishing identical conditions for every revision. NIAH results remain 99.1% single-hop and 31.3% CAP/25.4% QA multi-hop.

T1.justification: v3 Section 3.1 introduces the explicit definition T = min(Tmax, max(D, Tmin)), defines sampling density, and derives its short- and long-video regimes. v1 provides qualitative sampling guidance and experimental bounds. Other compression mathematics is largely re-expressed; neither version contains theoretical guarantees or proofs.

C1.justification: The abstract extends the leading-performance claim from 7B to both 2B and 7B and explicitly claims approximately 1/50 compression with almost no performance loss. v3 drops distributed training infrastructure as a distinct contribution. The central HiCo, LongVid, short-to-long learning, multi-hop benchmark, and 99.1% retrieval claims remain.

C2.justification: v3 emphasizes training-data leakage and memorization as weaknesses of single-hop NIAH, replacing v1's emphasis on visually distinctive needles. Section 6.1 adds an explanation that shallow attention selection can be biased before relevant locations are established. Table 6 also explicitly limits efficiency estimates to the LLM with precomputed visual features.

D1.justification: Supplementary Sections 7–8 add connector implementations, learning rates, batch sizes, epochs, trainable components, training-data sources, and detailed LongVid construction instructions. Table 6 specifies hardware and resource-estimation assumptions. These are largely new disclosures; Table 8 conflicts with retained prose on training sample counts and post-finetuning resolution, leaving exact reproduction uncertain.

R1.justification: v3 updates citations with Qwen2.5-VL, VITA1.5, DeepSpeed, and additional training-data sources, while removing grounding references such as VTimeLLM, HawkEye, and UniVTG. The principal positioning of HiCo relative to context extension and visual-token compression remains, with greater emphasis on the efficiency–performance balance.

P1.justification: The abstract, introduction, related work, and substantial method and experimental passages are rewritten. Dataset construction moves before the training section, compressor discussion shifts toward ablations and supplementary material, and the experimental narrative is consolidated. This substantially reorganizes the explanation beyond simply adding scientific content.

P2.justification: Figure 1 is redesigned around frame capacity and FLOP-sized bubbles. v3 consolidates benchmark and grounding results into a broader table, replaces the sampling table with plots, and adds diagnostic plots and qualitative panels. The compressor illustration is relocated from v1 Figure 4 to supplementary Figure 10 rather than newly introduced.

improvement.justification: v3 improves assessability through explicit sampling and data recipes, broader component ablations, and layerwise diagnostics unavailable in the supplied v1. However, Table 8 contradicts Section 3.3, including 4M versus 6M stage-2 samples and 224 versus 448 stage-4 resolution. Removing specialized temporal-grounding comparisons also narrows validation. The added explanation and evidence provide a net benefit, but unresolved reproducibility conflicts limit the overall quality gain.
